newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's landless marchers converge on capital.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's landless marchers converge on capital.

text.p: About 1,500 members of Brazil's radical Landless Movement (MST) converged on Brasilia on Monday on the last leg of a two-month trek to demand faster land reform.

A main column of weary demonstrators was due to enter the Federal District, which includes Brasilia, after walking nearly 750 miles (1,200 km) from the cities of Sao Paulo and Governador Valladares, Minas Gerais state.

A smaller group from western Mato Grosso state set up camp in a satellite city outside the capital on Sunday and began preparations for what organisers claim will be the biggest demonstration yet against President Fernando Henrique Cardoso.

Officials from trade union confederation CUT have said about 50,000 workers will join the protest. As well as the land issue, they will call on the government to suspend its privatisation programme and its plan to cut civil service jobs.

"We have to show the government how its economic policies are destroying the agricultural sector and throwing people out of work in the countryside and in the cities," MST director Gilberto Portes said.

The MST has emerged as one of Brazil's most potent opposition forces since it was founded in 1985 as an offshoot of a left-wing Catholic Church group working with rural labourers. By encouraging the landless to invade and cultivate unused farmland, the movement claims to have settled about 170,000 landless families. It says up to 5 million others, many of them in big city shantytowns, need land.

The land invasions have also aggravated Brazil's long-standing tensions over land, half of which belongs to just two percent of landowners. More than 100 people have been killed in land disputes during Cardoso's two-year term.
Thursday's demonstration marks the first anniversary of the killing by police of 19 landless workers seeking land in a remote corner of the Amazon. No one has yet been arrested for the massacre.
The government says its plan to settle 280,000 families in four years is the most ambitious in Brazil's history and has accused the MST of exploiting the land issue for its own political purposes.

Cardoso said on Sunday he would meet the leaders of the march in what would be the first talks between the government and the MST since August. But he sounded a warning note to those who expect a radical change in the government's policy.
"The land problem, which is as old as the country, cannot be resolved by one government. Perhaps not by a generation," Cardoso wrote in an article published on Monday by newspaper Gazeta Mercantil.
